paper.title: Metric Markov Cotype Two of ℓ1​
paper.html:
Abstract

We prove that the real Banach space ℓ1​ has metric Markov cotype two, answering a question of Mendel and Naor. As a consequence, every Lipschitz map from an arbitrary subset of a real Hilbert space into ℓ1​ extends to the whole Hilbert space with a universal multiplicative loss in its Lipschitz constant, resolving Ball's extension problem for this target.

1 Introduction

Metric Markov cotype asks whether the values of a map on a finite reversible Markov chain can be modified so that their one-step variation becomes small, while the cost of the modification is controlled by the original variation over a longer time interval. The modified values are not prescribed linear averages. This freedom is essential for the result proved here.
We work first with the real Banach space
ℓ1​={x=(x(k))k≥1​:k≥1∑​∣x(k)∣<∞},∥x∥1​=k≥1∑​∣x(k)∣.
Write N={1,2,…} and [n]={1,…,n}. A stochastic matrix A=(aij​)i,j∈[n]​ has nonnegative entries and each row sum equal to one. It is reversible with respect to a probability vector π=(πi​)i∈[n]​ if πi​aij​=πj​aji​ for all i,j. Reversibility implies stationarity, πA=π. Zero coordinates of π are allowed.
Definition 1.1 (Mendel–Naor).
A metric space (X,d) has metric Markov cotype two with constant C>0 if, for every n,t∈N, every probability vector π, every stochastic matrix A reversible with respect to π, and every x1​,…,xn​∈X, there exist y1​,…,yn​∈X such that
i∑​πi​d(xi​,yi​)2+ti,j∑​πi​aij​d(yi​,yj​)2≤C2i,j∑​πi​(t1​s=1∑t​As)ij​d(xi​,xj​)2.(1.1)
The infimum of all such constants is denoted N2​(X).
This is [4, Definition~1.2]. Our main result is the following.
Theorem 1.2.
The real space ℓ1​ satisfies
N2​(ℓ1​)≤1221​.
Thus the square of the constant in (1.1) may be taken to be 3024, independently of the number of points, the number of coordinates, and the time parameter. No optimization of this numerical constant is intended.

History and significance

Ball introduced Markov type and cotype in his study of Lipschitz extension [1]. His Markov cotype condition for Banach spaces uses specified linear averages, and ℓ1​ fails that stronger condition. Ball also proposed a metric definition. Mendel and Naor developed the Cesàro formulation above, proved its equivalence to Ball's metric definition, and asked explicitly whether N2​(ℓ1​) is finite [4, Question~1.15 and Section~7]. Theorem 1.2 answers that question affirmatively.
For 1<p≤2, the uniformly convex theory gives N2​(ℓp​)≤C/p−1​ with a universal constant C [1]; see also [4, Section~1.1]. These bounds deteriorate as p decreases to one and do not settle the endpoint treated here.
There is a second distinction worth making. Using a construction of Kalton, Mendel and Naor found a closed linear subspace of ℓ1​ that fails metric Markov cotype at every finite exponent [4, Theorem~1.14]. This does not rule out Theorem 1.2, because the points yi​ in Definition 1.1 need not belong to a given subspace containing the original data. Our construction uses this freedom.
One important consequence concerns extension of Lipschitz maps. For a map f between metric spaces, Lip(f) denotes the least L≥0 such that d(f(x),f(y))≤Ld(x,y) for all x,y in its domain. Ball's extension problem asks whether a Lipschitz map from an arbitrary subset of Hilbert space into ℓ1​ admits an extension with a universal multiplicative loss in its Lipschitz constant. Mendel and Naor explain that an affirmative answer to their metric Markov cotype question gives such an extension [4, Corollary~1.13 and the discussion after Question~1.15]. The extension problem is also discussed in [5, Section~1]. We record the consequence precisely in Section 6; the proof of Theorem 1.2 itself is elementary and independent of extension theorems.

The nonlinear construction

Finite subsets of ℓ1​ admit exact representations by weighted cuts; see [3]. We retain not only their distances but also a contractive map back to the given ambient ℓ1​. Nonlinear cut smoothing with the cubic ϕ(r)=3r2−2r3 also appears in the work of Cheng, Wang, and Xiang on sharp metric cotype [2]; metric cotype and metric Markov cotype are different invariants.
The additional ingredient here is a martingale estimate for the cubic. For a finite family B of cuts, the representation gives binary vectors zi​∈{0,1}B in a weighted Hilbert space H, with
∥zi​−zj​∥H2​=∥xi​−xj​∥1​.
It also gives a map T with T(zi​)=xi​ that is contractive for the weighted ℓ1​ norm on the cut coordinates. Let Q=[0,1]B, and let Φ:Q→Q apply ϕ coordinatewise. Stop an A-walk (Xs​) after an independent nonnegative geometric number S of steps with mean t. Writing Ei​ for expectation when the walk starts at i, we choose

For the estimate, start the walk from its stationary law π and record stopping as a separate transition after the S walk steps. Attach hj​ to the current index j while alive and zj​ when the walk stops at j, keeping that value thereafter. These values form a martingale. Because ϕ′ vanishes at the binary values, a fourth-power Hilbert potential controls the total squared weighted-ℓ1​ variation after applying Φ. Centering at zX0​​ makes the terminal potential equal to ∥xXS​​−xX0​​∥12​. The stopping jump accounts for the approximation cost, and the expected t preceding jumps account for the one-step variation. Contractivity of T transfers these bounds to ℓ1​.
We prove the cut representation in Section 2 and the martingale estimate in Section 3. The comparison in Section 4, valid in any metric space, converts the terminal geometric endpoint cost to the Cesàro average in (1.1). These ingredients are assembled in Section 5. The resulting points have a simple interpretation: each yi​ is the expected coordinatewise median of three independent geometric-walk endpoints started at i. This interpretation is established after the main proof.

For u,u′∈Q and e∈{0,1}B, put a=u−e, δ=u′−u, and Fe​(u)=∥u−e∥H4​. Then

4 Geometric and Cesàro endpoint costs

The stopped martingale will produce a geometric average of endpoint distances. The next estimate converts it to the finite average in Definition 1.1. We now construct the required points. Fix the data in Definition 1.1 with X=ℓ1​. If all xi​ coincide, choose yi​=xi​. Otherwise use Lemma 2.1 to obtain zi​,H,T, and use the map Φ of Section 3.
Put p=1/(t+1), q=1−p, and define

This convex combination converges in the finite-dimensional space H and belongs to Q. Equivalently, hi​=Ei​zXS​​, where Ei​ refers to an A-walk started at i and S is independent with P(S=s)=pqs. The first-step identity is

5.1 A martingale that realizes the two costs

Start a chain in an alive state with index distributed according to π. From an alive state of index i, it moves to the dead state of index i with probability p, and to the alive state of index j with probability qaij​. Dead states are absorbing. Its filtration Fm​ records the initial state and the first m transitions only.
One realization uses an independent stationary A-walk (Xs​)s≥0​ and successive independent survival trials, each successful with probability q. Let S be the number of successful trials before the first failure. Then P(S=s)=pqs and S is independent of the walk. There are S live index transitions followed by one death transition; the index at death is XS​.
Attach the value hi​ to the alive state of index i and the value zi​ to its dead state, and let Mm​ be the attached value at chain time m. Equation (5.2) shows that (Mm​) is an H-valued martingale for the indicated filtration. It lies in Q and is eventually constant almost surely, with

The vector e=zX0​​ is F0​-measurable and binary. Corollary 3.2 and (2.2) give

5.2 Completion of the proof

Proof of Theorem 1.2.
Use the points (5.3). Contractivity of T and the identity T(zi​)=xi​ imply

The proof uses reversibility only through πA=π. Consequently, the same inequality and the same construction hold for every stationary stochastic matrix, without detailed balance. No positivity assumption on the individual πi​ is needed in the argument.

5.3 An expected-median interpretation

The construction has an intrinsic description in the original coordinates. Let
G=ps=0∑∞​qsAs
be the stochastic matrix of geometric endpoints. For fixed i, take independent indices J1​,J2​,J3​ with common law P(Ja​=j)=Gij​. For three real vectors, write med(x,x′,x′′) for their coordinatewise median. This vector belongs to ℓ1​, since its coordinatewise absolute value is at most ∣x∣+∣x′∣+∣x′′∣. Then
yi​=Emed(xJ1​​,xJ2​​,xJ3​​).(5.6)
In each original coordinate, the median is at least a given threshold exactly when at least two of the three values are. The threshold decomposition in the proof of Lemma 2.1 therefore gives the pointwise identity

Each indicator has expectation 3hi​(B)2(1−hi​(B))+hi​(B)3=ϕ(hi​(B)). Taking expectations in the finite sum proves (5.6).

6 Complex scalars and Lipschitz extension

Corollary 6.1.
For complex scalars, N2​(ℓ1​(C))≤1242​.
Proof.
The real-linear bijection
J:ℓ1​(C)⟶ℓ1​(R),Jx=(ℜx(1),ℑx(1),ℜx(2),ℑx(2),…)
satisfies ∥x∥1​≤∥Jx∥1​≤2​∥x∥1​. Apply Theorem 1.2 to Jxi​ and pull the resulting points back by J−1. The left side of (1.1) can only decrease, while its right side increases by at most a factor of 2.
∎
For the extension consequence, recall that a metric space (Z,dZ​) has Markov type two with constant M>0 if
i,j∑​πi​(At)ij​dZ​(ui​,uj​)2≤M2ti,j∑​πi​aij​dZ​(ui​,uj​)2
for every n,t∈N, every stochastic matrix A reversible with respect to a probability vector π, and every u1​,…,un​∈Z. Hilbert spaces satisfy this inequality with M=1 [1]; see also [4, Definition~1.1 and the following discussion].
Corollary 6.2.
There is a universal constant K<∞ such that, for every real Hilbert space H, every subset S⊆H, and every Lipschitz map f:S→ℓ1​, there is an extension F:H→ℓ1​ with Lip(F)≤KLip(f).
Proof.
We use the Lipschitz extension theorem in [4, Corollary~1.13], extending Ball's theorem [1]. In its Banach-space form, a source with Markov type two and a dual Banach target with metric Markov cotype two admit extensions with a constant bounded by a universal multiple of the two corresponding constants. A Hilbert space has Markov type two with constant one, and ℓ1​ is the dual of c0​. Theorem 1.2 verifies the remaining hypothesis.
∎
